Once you're in a descent you have to see it through; a jump you simply decline. So only jump what you can already jump, and don't jump much at the start.

There is no version of this where the rush arrives without the danger attached. On a fast descent there is no cage, no harness, nothing between you and the road - a fairground ride always keeps some safety, and this keeps none.

https://rollerskateaesthetic.com/skate/adrenaline-comes-with-danger/

Written with AI from a skater's notes.

Experienced skaters are blunt about this one: you don't take a city centre as a beginner. The gate is not how brave you feel, it's whether your braking and your turning are perfect - not adequate, perfect - because traffic doesn't wait for you to assemble a stop.

https://rollerskateaesthetic.com/skate/city-skating-is-not-for-beginners/

Drafted with AI, based on a skater's notes.

Before you glide: marching, the duck walk, then the glide. V stance, bent knees - and you skip the backwards fall everyone takes on day one.

https://rollerskateaesthetic.com/skate/first-three-moves/

AI-written from notes by a skater. This page contains affiliate links.

Once a hill is steep, trying to brake is worse than riding it out, at every level. Keep your wheels as straight as you can, knees bent, feel the tarmac, and make no movement you don't need - the steeper it gets, the more any gesture costs.

https://rollerskateaesthetic.com/skate/hills-you-do-not-brake/

Made with AI from real skating notes.

Most beginner pain comes from a bad fit, not from falling. Measure in millimetres, follow the brand's own chart, then fasten the skate firmly.

https://rollerskateaesthetic.com/skate/how-to-size-roller-skates/

Written with AI from a skater's notes. Some links on this page are affiliate links.

Both skates stay down. Your ankle is locked inside a rigid boot, so it cannot tilt - the lean comes from the whole leg, knees bent, weight over the wheels.

https://rollerskateaesthetic.com/skate/how-to-turn-on-skates/

Drafted with AI, based on a skater's notes.

Face forward, hold a wall, and push your heels apart then together - the same shape as a plow stop, done in reverse. Look over one shoulder, never straight down.

https://rollerskateaesthetic.com/skate/skating-backwards-first-steps/

AI-written from notes by a skater.

Cheap skates hurt whether they are new or worn in, and no amount of wearing them fixes it. Good ones still ache at first, because a rigid inline boot is rigid.

https://rollerskateaesthetic.com/skate/why-skates-hurt/

Falling forward onto your knee pads and wrist guards is the safe fall - you see it coming and can even roll out of it. Falling backwards onto your tailbone or head is the one that hurts.

A hard inline boot locks your ankle, so the skate becomes an extension of your leg - standing still and rolling alike. Quads win on tight turns and rink dancing, but that is manoeuvrability, not stability.

https://rollerskateaesthetic.com/skate/inline-skates-are-more-stable/?src=threads

Wet ground doesn't take away all your stopping power, it takes away one particular kind: anything that turns a wheel across your direction of travel. Dragging a foot behind you keeps the wheels roughly in line and still works.

https://rollerskateaesthetic.com/skate/never-turn-a-wheel-sideways-on-wet/?src=threads

A pastel skate aesthetic is a palette, not a purchase: soft coral, lilac, sage and butter against cream, with one darker line to stop it going washed out. The cheapest way in is laces, toe caps and wheels, three small reversible swaps.

https://rollerskateaesthetic.com/skate/pastel-skate-aesthetic/?src=threads

The plow stop is the easiest stop to learn: roll with feet a little wider than your hips, push your heels apart so the toes turn in, bend your knees and press down and outward through the whole foot. Both feet stay down, so no single-leg balance is needed.

https://rollerskateaesthetic.com/skate/plow-stop/?src=threads

Made with AI from real skating notes. The page includes affiliate links.

Everyone leans back the first time, and everyone falls. Rolling backwards keeps the pressure on the front of your skates, exactly as it does going forwards, and that is the part nobody expects.

https://rollerskateaesthetic.com/skate/backwards-weight-stays-forward/?src=threads

Written with AI from a skater's notes.

Pronation on skates — the boot rolling onto its inside edge on every step — is a joint problem, not a style one. Left alone, it leads to slow-onset injuries in the ankle, knee or hip on that side.

https://rollerskateaesthetic.com/skate/pronation-is-an-injury-problem/?src=threads

Six of the seven voices in our compilation who talk about plate material back aluminium: four ride a Powerdyne Reactor (Bonnie Thunders, Suzy Hotrod, Caro Hernandez, Kid Ace) and coach Lisa J tells beginners metal, never plastic.

https://rollerskateaesthetic.com/guide/aluminium-vs-nylon-skate-plates/?src=threads

The wheel that slips out on wet ground is usually not the one you're rolling on, it's the one you just shoved off with. A hard push loads a wheel sideways for a fraction of a second, and sideways is exactly what wet ground won't give you.

https://rollerskateaesthetic.com/skate/dont-push-hard-on-wet-ground/?src=threads

To get up on roller skates, get onto all fours, bring one skate flat under you so the knee points up, put both hands on that knee and press up to standing, weight over your feet. It is a sequence, not a fitness move, and you will use it dozens of times in your first month.

https://rollerskateaesthetic.com/skate/how-to-get-up/?src=threads

Skates are built to be rolled on wet roads, and getting them wet is not the mistake. Zipping them straight into a bag afterwards is.
